fields.connection: Vたら + いかがですか（more polite than たらどうですか）
examples: If you're not feeling well, why don't you have a doctor look at you at the hospital?
If you're lost, why don't you ask at the police box?
How about proceeding with this plan?
If you like, why don't you have a seat here?
Why don't you consult an expert once?
How about leaving a bit earlier?
fields.explain:
Place it after a condition/situation to sound friendly: もしお急ぎなら、先にお食事され たらいかがですか。
Combine with cushion phrases:恐れ入りますが／よろしければ／差し支えなければ + Vたらいかがですか。
With customers/partners: polite, but avoid pressuring; it is good to offer another option.
With your boss/superiors, it is still polite but can imply "you should do it"; consider the form that asks for their opinion: 〜いかがでしょうか。

• Makes a suggestion/proposal politely: "How about …?"
• Often used in service/business settings or when you need to save the other person's face.
• Compared with 〜たらどうですか: less direct and less imposing; but it is still a suggestion, so avoid it with sensitive topics.
fields.notes:
• In written proposals, “〜いかがでしょうか” is more polite than “〜いかがですか”.
• Combining it with keigo sounds natural: お試しになったらいかがですか／ご検討いかがでしょうか。
• Avoid it with extreme suggestions or ones that may cause loss of face: × 会社を辞めたらいかがですか (too strong/harsh).
mistakes: Confusing it with an invitation: 〜ませんか means “do it together”, while 〜たらいかがですか means “suggest that the listener do it”.
Using it for sensitive topics can be impolite even though the form is polite. Choose a more indirect expression if necessary.
Confusing the politeness level with 〜たらどうですか: JLPT questions often test the difference in nuance.

examples: If you have a headache, why don't you go to bed early today?
Why don't you ask the teacher about the parts you don't understand?
Why don't you just throw those shoes away? They've got a hole in them.
How about starting with small goals first?
Why don't you stop pushing yourself so hard at work? Your health is what matters.
fields.explain:
Neutral/polite: ～たらどうですか／～たらいかがですか.
Casual: ～たらどう？／～たら？; requires a close relationship and a soft intonation so as not to sound rude.
Not used when the speaker has no "grounds" to give advice (to avoid sounding tactless). It should be tied to a specific situation.
To advise "not doing" something: express it indirectly with やめる/控える/ないでおく + たらどう.

• A suggestion/advice like "How about …?" or "Why don't you …?", based on a difficulty/problem the listener is facing.
• Strength: softer than a command, stronger than the invitation question ～ませんか (because it implies "you should do it").
• The nuance can become critical/nagging if the intonation is emphatic or the context is tense (やめたらどう？ sometimes sounds like "why don't you just give it up?").
• Often used after hearing the listener's problem, to offer a practical suggestion.
fields.notes:
• You can add もう/とりあえず to soften it: とりあえず休んだらどう？
• In business emails, prefer ～たらいかがでしょうか／ご検討いただけますか to stay polite.
• When the listener is older/a superior: avoid ～たらどう？ as it can easily be rude.
mistakes: Incorrect: × 食べなかったらどう？ to advise “don't eat” → Use 食べないでおいたらどう？
Using it casually with strangers/superiors → sounds rude. Choose いかがでしょうか.
Confusing its function with the invitation ～ませんか. ～たらどうですか is advice, not necessarily an invitation to do something together.

rows: A direct suggestion, with a nuance of “should”.
<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったらどうですか。
States the norm “should/should not” more clearly.
もっと<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>たほうがいい。
Focuses on doing something together; polite, no implication of “should”.
<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きませんか。
Short; can easily become criticism if not used tactfully.

fields.meaning: Expresses that the condition in the first clause being met is the starting point for something new to happen or for a new discovery.
examples: When I woke up, my face looked terrible.
When I didn't stop at the traffic light, I got pulled over by the police.
When I said I was going back to my country, my girlfriend cried.
When I went to school, it was closed because of the typhoon.
On my days off, I do things like read books and watch movies.
It keeps raining on and off.
He is someone who is happy one moment and sad the next.
On my business trip, I went to places like Osaka and Nagoya.
Prices at this store are sometimes high and sometimes low.
fields.explain:
It is a representative listing, not an exhaustive one. You can add ほかに to emphasize "there are other things too".
In spoken language, する at the end is often dropped if the context is clear, but the standard form should have する.
Expresses "sometimes/occasionally" when there is only one part + したりする.

• Lists representative actions/states non-exhaustively: "sometimes … sometimes …", "do things like … and …".
• Often expresses repetition, change, or representative examples; does not emphasize order.
• The tense and repetition/habit/past are determined by the ending する (します／しました／している).
• You can use only one part + したりする to say "also … sometimes": 甘いものを食べたりする。
fields.notes:
• り can be combined three or more times if needed, but two parts are the most common.
• In describing symptoms/weather, ～たり～たりする expresses fluctuation very naturally.
• Replace する with しています to express an ongoing present state.
mistakes: Dropping する in standard written language: × 読んだり見たり。→ 読んだり見たりする。
Wrong tense: 読んだり見たりしました is correct if the sentence is in the past tense.
Wrong word form: × 安いだり → 安かったり; × 便利だり → 便利だったり。

rows: Not exhaustive; tense decided by する.

Close in meaning to “both … and …”; different function.
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いし<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>だし
More casual and vaguer than たり.

examples: I can only speak Japanese.
There is nothing but water here.
Only buses run in this town.
We only have one hour, so let's hurry.
I'm sorry I can only help this much.
It's an event that only elementary school students can enter.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker feels the amount/target is small, limited, or unsatisfactory.
Often used with verbs of existence/ability: ある／いる／できる／わかる／話せる…
In polite language: 〜だけしか ありません／ありませんでした .
If you want to be neutral (no implication of insufficiency), use Nだけ + affirmative:水だけあります。

• "Only … and nothing else": a strong limitation structure, with a nuance of insufficiency/regret.
• だけしか is always used with a verb/predicate in the negative form: Vない/ありません/いない.
• Compared with だけ (neutral), だけしか (= しか + ない with the particle だけ for emphasis) carries stronger emotion.
• Close in meaning to Nしか + Vない; だけしか leans toward spoken language, is more emphatic, and is sometimes grammatically redundant but natural.
fields.notes:
• Grammatically, だけしか is double emphasis (だけ + しか + ない); although it seems redundant, it is a natural expression in spoken language.
• だけしか is not used in the pattern “Vるしかない” (have no choice but to) because that is a different pattern: もう行くしかない。
• It can be combined with the topic particle: 彼だけしかは来なかった（rarely used, be careful with the rhythm; more natural: 彼しか来なかった）. explain: Used to express the idea of something being the only one, unique ⏐ examples: 1. このコンサートは、会員だけしか入れません。
Only members can enter this concert.
2. 今日はお客様が一人だけしか来ませんでした。
Only one customer came today.
mistakes: Using it with an affirmative: × 水だけしかあります → √ 水だけあります or 水だけしかありません。
Confusing the nuance with だけ: “水だけある” does not carry the sense of insufficiency that “水だけしかない” does.
Dropping the negative at the end of the sentence because “しか” is already there: × 彼だけしか来た → √ 彼だけしか来なかった。
Using “しか…ない” and “だけ” redundantly in different positions is confusing: prefer either NしかVない or NだけしかVない.

fields.meaning:
start an action or event
complete an action or event.
continue an action or behavior
fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + だす/はじめる/おわる/つづける
examples: On my way home, it started to rain.
The child suddenly burst out crying, so I was surprised and asked why.
Even though I didn't do anything, the elevator suddenly started moving.
It's already been three years since I started learning the piano, but I'm just not getting any better.
I started doing my homework after watching the 10 o'clock news, so I went to bed late.
I started reading this book last month, but I still haven't finished it.

fields.name: ～ちゃう［contracted form］
examples: I overslept this morning.
You actually said something like that to a woman?
fields.explain: ◎ A contracted sentence pattern of「でしまう」, used in spoken language.

fields.meaning: indicates manner | indicates cause | connects two actions
examples: Every morning I put on a tie and go to work.
The building collapsed because of the earthquake.
Sorry I'm late.
I'm sorry for being so noisy.
I'm not very bright, so I don't really understand.
I've lost my wallet and I'm in trouble.
fields.explain:
～て： indicates a cause. The second clause is the result arising from that cause.
V/Aて:
The second clause is not a volitional expression but a word expressing a feeling or mood, such as relief, surprise, sadness, joy…, or it may also be a word expressing ability or a state.
Nで:
The noun in this case is a noun for a natural phenomenon, incident, or event, such as じこ、じしん、かじ…

① Listing actions:Used to connect actions that happen one after another in chronological order.
→ "and then…", "and after that…"
② Simultaneous / parallel:Expresses two actions happening at the same time.
→ "while…"
③ Cause / reason:Used to express a mild reason for an emotion or result.
→ "because…, so…"
④ Manner / means:Describes the means or way of doing something.
→ "by…", "in the state of…"
fields.notes:
The te-form is one of the most basic verb forms, the foundation for dozens of other grammar points (～てください, ～てもいい, ～てはいけない, ～ている...).
Mastering the te-form makes it easy to link several actions and build natural sentences in conversation.
At N5 level, learners should master the 3 main usages: connecting actions, indicating a mild cause, and manner/simultaneity.
mistakes: Wrong te-form conjugation:行きて (incorrect) →行って(correct)。
Confusing Vて with Vてから — て only connects, てから emphasizes “after”.
Forgetting to conjugate the tense on the last verb: ✕食べて行くました → ○食べて行きました。
JLPT N5 often tests: te-form conjugation, choosing correctly between て・てから・それから.

◎ Gives permission even if it is like that.
◎ It can be used with verbs, in which case it becomes「～てもかまわない」.
fields.notes: Expresses concession. It means that although something is not the best, you compromise and accept it as good enough. As in ⑨, when there are several options, it indicates the range of what is acceptable. It can be rephrased as 「…てもいい」.（２８０）

examples: When you take time off, you have to let us know.

fields.explain: ◎ Like「~なければならない」, it indicates things that cannot be avoided, such as obligations.

examples: You don't have to take everything.
I don't mind if I can't go.
fields.explain: ◎ Not doing that does not matter; it is not a problem.

examples: If it's drinks, I've already bought them.
If you need a dentist, I know a good one.
If you're going to study abroad, it's best to do it while you're young.
"Excuse me, is Kim here?" "If you mean Kim, Kim just went home a little while ago."
"What about the scissors I lent you earlier?" "The scissors? I put them back in the drawer."
"I'm thinking of going to a hot spring or something during the long weekend next month."
fields.explain:
◎ A hypothetical condition sentence pattern; the second clause is usually a statement of judgment; used with nouns, adjectives, and verbs in the dictionary form.

after hearing what the other person says, then say what you know about it. Said as an opinion, a hope, or a request.
(hearing a lot of information from the other person), then giving an opinion about it. In terms of chronological order, the action proposed last will be the one that comes first.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: An expression used when the speaker receives information ~ and then gives their own judgment or opinion, or calls on/urges the other person to act. The ~ part is the topic raised in the conversation or a topic obtained from observing the other person's situation.
examples: 1. ①サラ「ケーキがおいしい店を知りませんか。」
山田「ケーキなら、駅前のセボンがおいしいですよ。」
Sara: "Do you know a shop with good cakes?"
Yamada: "For cakes, Sebon in front of the station is really good."
2. ②トム「春休みに京都に行きたいです。」
先生「京都に行くなら、ガイドブックをかしましょうか。」
Tom: "I want to go to Kyoto during spring break."
Teacher: "If you're going to Kyoto, shall I lend you a guidebook?"
3. ③【テレビがついているが、子供は見ていない】
[The TV is on, but the child isn't watching it.]
Mom: "If you're not watching it, I'll turn the TV off, OK?"

fields.meaning: Depending on, due to, by means of | caused by ~
examples: This work was painted by a famous artist.
Many buildings collapsed due to the earthquake.
We identify customer needs through surveys.
Culture differs greatly from country to country.
Depending on the circumstances, the meeting will be postponed.
The accuracy of AI-based machine translation has improved.
fields.explain:
More formal than で (means) and から/ために (cause).
In the passive, “NによってV-られる” is the formula for indicating a natural agent.
“によっては” is often used with a clause giving a representative example/exception.
“により”/“による” often appear in announcements and official documents.

• Agent of a passive sentence: “by …”.
• Cause/driving force: “due to/because of …” (usually formal, major events, objective).
• Method/means/basis: “by/through …”.
• Dependence/variation: “depending on …, … differs”.
• “によっては”: presents one branch among many possibilities that may occur.
fields.notes:
• For natural disasters/major incidents as the cause, prefer “によって/により”; for ordinary/volitional causes use “で/ために”.
• Announcement style: “台風により全便欠航のお知らせ”.
• “人によっては” is a very natural pattern for stating individual differences. meaning_vi: By means of, due to, because of, depending on ⏐ explain: Used to express the method, cause, or case for each action or event ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は努力によって病気を克服した！
He overcame his illness through his own effort!
2. 人によって考え方が違います。
Ways of thinking differ from person to person.
3. 台風によって屋根が飛ばされた。
The roof was blown off by the typhoon.
mistakes: Using “によって” as the agent in an active sentence (unnatural): use agent + が/は for active sentences.
For everyday causes, “で/から/ために” is more natural: 風邪で会社を休む (avoid: 風邪によって).
Confusing “によっては” with “によって”: “によっては” must be followed by a specific example/branch.
Forgetting the formal variants in documents: “により/による” are appropriate for announcements/policies.

fields.meaning: Nominalization | It's because…, the thing is…
fields.connection: V/A plain form + のだ / N・Na + なのだ
examples: "Now we're free at last!" That's what everyone thought.
It's precisely because I studied a little every day that I was able to pass like this.
I'm sorry I left early yesterday. I was a little tired.
That way of doing it isn't good. You just need to do it like this.
"Why were you absent yesterday?" "I had a headache."
"Who broke this glass?" "I'm sorry, it was me."
fields.explain:
“んです” is natural in conversation; “のです” is more formal/academic.
Questions with のですか/んですか are soft and show interest rather than interrogation.
Starting a request/suggestion with “～んですが、…” makes it polite and indirect.
Avoid overusing “のです” in formal written language when the explanatory nuance is not needed.

• “～のです/んです” adds an explanatory nuance, presents background, emphasizes a reason or background information.
• Used when the speaker thinks the listener needs/wants to know “the reason/what is behind the matter”.
• Used in questions to gently ask for an explanation: どうして来なかったんですか。
• Used to soften a request/suggestion when set up as a premise: 実は、明日忙しいんですが…
• Compared with an ordinary statement, のです gives the sentence a sense of “explaining/wrapping up/emphasis”.
fields.notes:
• のです after a nominalized clause: ～のは…のです is used to define/explain clearly.
• Tense/past: ～だったんです/～ていたんです helps make clear that something has happened.
• Avoid using it with direct commands; when needed, put のですが in the introductory clause to be more polite.
mistakes: Forgetting な: 静かのです× → 静かなのです✓; 学生のです× → 学生なのです✓
Mistaking “んですか” for a harsh question; in fact it is polite, but the intonation needs to be soft.
Overusing のです in written language makes sentences heavy; the JLPT often tests where the explanatory nuance is or is not needed.
Confusing it with わけです (logical conclusion) → のです only explains and does not always imply inference.
